title: Prefrontal · Governed context as a product
subtitle: Leadership value to developer contract

slides.title: Approve context once. Reuse it with control.
slides.lead: Turn business knowledge into approved, linked context for the analytics and AI applications you already use.

items.title: One reusable context layer
items.text: Build on Looker, LookML, Zenlytics and custom apps.

items.title: A funded proof of value
items.text: Start with one workflow. Measure the return before expansion.

slides.note: Product concept and pilot proposal. Writing inspired by ASD-STE100; full compliance has not been checked.

slides.title: Your AI keeps paying to understand the same work.
slides.lead: Your stack already models data. The proposal addresses context that teams still reconcile across tools, owners and versions.

items.title: Preparation
items.text: People connect existing metric definitions to evidence, exceptions and ownership.

items.title: Reconciliation
items.text: People resolve conflicting versions and missing conditions.

items.title: Review and rework
items.text: People check unsupported or unsuitable outputs.

items.title: Change management
items.text: Teams reconnect context when models or tools change.

slides.note: These are problem hypotheses. Establish their frequency and cost in the selected workflow.

slides.title: One governed context service. Many consumers.
slides.lead: The product accepts submissions, governs meaning, organizes linked records and delivers permitted context.

items.title: Reusable asset
items.text: Link approved source definitions to reusable records. Preserve native query execution.

items.title: Clear product boundary
items.text: Your applications consume context and control their own actions.

slides.note: Proposed workflow. Human approval and access controls must work before context reaches a consumer.

nodes.title: Submit context
nodes.detail: People and agent loops submit evidence in one structured template. The original source remains available.

nodes.title: Approve meaning
nodes.detail: A responsible human checks meaning, evidence and access. Approval binds to the exact version.

nodes.title: Build linked layers
nodes.detail: The context agent organizes approved records. Stable IDs connect the layers. New meaning returns to review.

nodes.title: Serve context
nodes.detail: The delivery server checks the caller and the requested records. Your applications decide how to use permitted outputs.

slides.title: The product must earn back its overhead.
slides.lead: Reuse the current stack. Fund a bounded pilot only when accepted value can repay the added setup and operations.

items.title: Cost
items.text: Compare full cost per accepted task.

items.title: Performance
items.text: Measure complete delivery time and tail latency.

items.title: Accuracy
items.text: Review source support and preserved meaning.

items.title: Trust
items.text: Prove access boundaries and audit readback.

slides.note: Illustrative hurdle, not a price quote or forecast. The pilot must establish whether the required benefit is achievable.

slides.title: From a submission to a permitted context output.
slides.lead: One workflow connects human governance, stable identities, linked layers and secure delivery. Feedback starts a new submission.
slides.note: Proposed architecture. Consumer applications execute their own workflows. The context layer does not grant them action authority.

slides.title: Govern context across your existing stack.
slides.lead: Keep LookML as the approved metric source. Add portable context governance across Looker, Zenlytics and custom apps.

items.title: Existing foundation
items.text: Looker and LookML provide modeled analytics. Zenlytics and custom apps already serve your workflows.

items.title: Proposed addition
items.text: Shared record contracts, approval history and permitted delivery. Verify each adapter before use.

slides.note: Reported current stack. Adapters and live integration remain unverified. Native query execution stays in Looker and the warehouse.

flow.title: Proposed integration with the current analytics stack

nodes.title: LookML source
nodes.detail: LookML defines dimensions, measures and relationships. Reference the approved model, Explore, view and field, or certified SQL. Keep native query execution.

nodes.title: Context passport
nodes.detail: A metric passport links canonical identity, source revision, population, grain, unit, time window, exceptions and access. Human review approves the exact version.

nodes.title: Delivery adapter
nodes.detail: An adapter translates between contracts. Verify the actual API or MCP interface, caller identity, source permissions, expiry and revocation. An adapter does not inherit permissions automatically.

nodes.title: Existing consumers
nodes.detail: Consumers receive permitted context through their verified interface. A custom app can support submission and review. The consumer controls its own query and action execution.

slides.title: Make every submission reviewable.
slides.lead: Use one structured envelope. Let the interface show it as a table. Keep the original source beside the proposed record.

items.title: Preserve meaning
items.text: Retain dates, units, negation, exceptions and uncertainty.

items.title: Check before review
items.text: Reject malformed input. Hold unsupported or conflicting claims.

slides.note: Illustrative schema and record. Source content supplies evidence; it cannot change system policy.

slides.title: Clear language carries the original meaning.
slides.lead: Use STE-inspired text to help people review context. Structured fields carry the checks that prose cannot enforce.

items.title: Keep two views
items.text: Store the original text and the clearer review view.

items.title: Keep every condition
items.text: Preserve the 30-day rule and the dispute exception.

items.title: Review the transformation
items.text: A fluent rewrite can still change meaning.

items.title: Use one term
items.text: Use the same term for the same governed concept.

slides.note: ASD-STE100 is a controlled writing specification. STE-inspired prose does not establish full compliance or factual correctness.

slides.title: Approval is a decision about an exact version.
slides.lead: A responsible reviewer accepts, rejects or requests changes. The model can propose a record; it cannot approve its own meaning.

items.title: Evidence review
items.text: Check sources, dates, scope and unsupported statements.

items.title: Meaning review
items.text: Check definitions, units, assumptions and conflicts.

items.title: Access review
items.text: Confirm workspace, permitted audience and purpose.

items.title: Version-bound approval
items.text: Bind the reviewer decision to the submitted content hash.

items.title: Derived claims
items.text: Send new interpretation through preparation and review.

items.title: Release ownership
items.text: An accountable owner accepts release and pilot evidence.

slides.note: HITL means human in the loop. All new or changed meaning requires review in this proposed admission workflow.

slides.title: Stable identities connect every layer.
slides.lead: A canonical ID names one governed object. A version names its state. Evidence references explain where that state came from.

items.title: Resolve identity
items.text: Match the existing object before creating another canonical ID.

items.title: Bind the semantic source
items.text: For metrics, map the LookML model, Explore, view and measure to a Git revision.

items.title: Version the meaning
items.text: Keep the owner, approval, population, grain, unit, time window and exceptions with each version.

items.title: Enforce permissions
items.text: An ID locates a record. Recheck access for each consumer and source query.

slides.note: A metric passport is a governed record of a metric definition and its source binding. Reference the approved LookML formula; avoid a competing copy.

slides.title: Separate facts, measures, concepts and interpretation.
slides.lead: Each layer answers a different question. Canonical IDs join the layers inside a controlled workspace.

items.title: Semantic layers
items.text: These are categories of meaning, not a requirement for four databases.

items.title: Governed links
items.text: Derived records reference approved input IDs and versions.

slides.note: The arrows show relationships between categories. They do not require every submission to pass through all four layers.

flow.title: Four semantic layers share governed identities

nodes.title: Data
nodes.detail: The Data layer records source facts, fields and values. It preserves source versions, dates and units.

nodes.title: Metric
nodes.detail: The Metric layer references the approved LookML measure or certified SQL revision. It records population, grain, unit and period, and links Data IDs. It does not replace native calculation logic.

nodes.title: Ontology
nodes.detail: An ontology defines concepts and their relationships. It connects aliases to governed entity IDs.

nodes.title: Interpretation
nodes.detail: The Interpretation layer explains what the records mean under stated assumptions. Reviewers approve new derived claims.

slides.eyebrow: Developer view · your model and harness
slides.title: Typed decisions. Human authority.
slides.lead: A harness is application code that checks model outputs and limits allowed operations.

items.title: Choice
items.text: Select one category from an allowed list.

items.title: Yes / no
items.text: Judge a defined condition. Policy checks still enforce access.

items.title: Rubric score
items.text: Rate a property against stated criteria. A score is not a probability.

items.title: Calibration
items.text: Check reported probabilities against observed outcomes before using risk thresholds.

slides.note: For familiar questions, deliver certified query references for native execution after access checks. New questions use expert drafts and review. The three decision types remain proposed; JEV parity and calibration are unverified.

slides.title: Keep records durable. Keep task context bounded.
slides.lead: A context vault is a workspace with controlled records and access rules. A consumer receives a permitted view, not the whole vault.

items.title: Canonical records
items.text: Keep sources, approved versions, status and review history.

items.title: Derived views
items.text: Build search indexes, graphs or caches when a use case needs them.

items.title: Working context
items.text: Load relevant subject matter expert (SME) knowledge within the request budget.

items.title: Corrections
items.text: Invalidate dependent views when inputs expire, change or lose access.

slides.note: The semantic layers describe meaning. This storage lifecycle describes persistence and retrieval. A cache is never an approval authority.

slides.title: Deliver context through an explicit access boundary.
slides.lead: The MCP server exposes permitted context. The server must enforce the product’s record and workspace policies.

items.title: Structured output
items.text: Return IDs, versions, evidence, validity and unresolved limits.

items.title: Access at use
items.text: Recheck permissions for each resource or tool request.

slides.note: MCP defines context exchange. Authentication and application authorization still require implementation. The protocol alone does not make a product secure.

flow.title: A context request crosses explicit access checks

nodes.title: Identify caller
nodes.detail: Authenticate the caller. Resolve the requested workspace and purpose. Authentication establishes identity.

nodes.title: Authorize records
nodes.detail: Authorization decides which records the caller may access. Check current approval, expiry and withdrawal.

nodes.title: Assemble output
nodes.detail: Return only permitted records and evidence references. Include version, validity and unresolved limits. Enforce a response budget.

nodes.title: Deliver through MCP
nodes.detail: MCP means Model Context Protocol. It connects the server to consuming applications. Application actions remain under consumer authority.

slides.eyebrow: Developer view · adapting to new technology
slides.title: Keep the knowledge. Qualify each replacement.
slides.lead: Versioned contracts let us evaluate new models, retrieval systems and interfaces while preserving governed context.

items.title: Durable asset
items.text: Meaning, evidence and approved identities survive component changes.

items.title: Qualification cost
items.text: Budget evaluation, migration, rollback and maintenance.

slides.note: Adaptability is a design objective. No architecture can guarantee that future technology will never surpass it.

flow.title: Replace components through a qualification gate

nodes.title: Keep the contract
nodes.detail: Treat governed records and their contracts as durable assets. A new adapter must preserve meaning, evidence and access rules.

nodes.title: Connect a candidate
nodes.detail: Introduce a candidate behind the same interface. Record its version and configuration. Do not assume a familiar interface preserves behavior.

nodes.title: Compare outcomes
nodes.detail: Evaluate the candidate on held-out cases, boundary failures and complete task cost. Keep development cases separate.

nodes.title: Release or retain
nodes.detail: Release only after the owner accepts the evidence. Retain the prior compatible release on failure. Invalidate affected caches when dependencies change.

slides.eyebrow: The investment · where the money goes
slides.title: Count the whole operating process.
slides.lead: A context layer can add review, storage and maintenance cost. It creates value only when accepted outcomes repay that cost.

items.title: Setup
items.text: Record contract, source mapping, adapters, deployment and acceptance tests.

items.title: Recurring platform
items.text: Tokens, warehouse queries, storage, tools, delivery and monitoring.

items.title: Human operations
items.text: Submission review, conflict resolution, corrections and incident handling.

items.title: Maintenance
items.text: Licenses, seats, source updates, access changes, upgrades and recovery.

slides.note: Separate existing allocated costs from incremental spending. Include both consistently in the baseline and candidate. Count each cost once.

slides.title: Spend less only when the accepted result stays sound.
slides.lead: The updated plan supplies optimization candidates. Test them against the current workflow before claiming a benefit.

items.title: Reuse approved code or SQL
items.text: Use deterministic logic for defined rules. Keep certified queries unchanged. Review expert drafts before reuse.

items.title: Bound context and output
items.text: Limit permitted context, tokens, output, steps and retries. Batch work only when its deadline permits.

items.title: Reuse valid context
items.text: Check cache version, expiry, access and invalidation. Measure hit rate, writes, reads and storage.

items.title: Qualify the model route
items.text: Use a smaller model only if it passes the task gates. Escalate uncertain results.

items.title: Control warehouse cost
items.text: Estimate query work. For BigQuery on-demand queries, test maximum bytes billed. A row limit alone may not bound scans.

items.title: Count every cost once
items.text: Track tokens, queries, seats, licenses and human review. Assign budget owners. Separate existing and incremental costs.

slides.note: These are proposed controls. The supplied v6 best practices remain unapproved team guidance. No percentage saving, vendor price or achieved product improvement is claimed.

slides.title: Change the assumptions. Inspect the return.
slides.lead: Compare the same accepted-task target. The starting example assumes no improvement and therefore shows added cost.
slides.note: Invented assumptions in USD. Test a positive case and a higher-cost case. Financial results never override quality or permission gates.

slides.title: Agree the proof before paying for scale.
slides.lead: Run a baseline and a candidate on the same workload. Use held-out cases and complete cost evidence.
slides.note: Proposed pilot measurements. No product result has been measured. An accepted task passes owner criteria. p95 covers 95% of measured completion times.

slides.title: See what a component change must preserve.
slides.lead: Run four browser scenarios on one record. Inspect evidence loss, exception loss and expanded permission.

items.title: What works today
items.text: The presentation executes these deterministic example checks.

items.title: What the prototype must add
items.text: A real submission, review, persisted release and authenticated context read.

slides.note: A browser rehearsal demonstrates the intended contract. It does not validate a model, server, database or operational outcome.

slides.title: The pitch is ready. The runtime still needs proof.
slides.lead: We can fund implementation against a visible architecture and explicit acceptance cases. We cannot yet sell proven operating results.

items.title: Available now
items.text: The presentation and worksheet. The current analytics stack is reported by the team.

items.title: Designed
items.text: Submission governance, canonical identities, semantic layers and controlled delivery.

items.title: To implement
items.text: Source adapters, persistent governance, model harness, authorization and MCP delivery.

items.title: To qualify
items.text: Live integration, calibration, access isolation, recovery, load and buyer return.

slides.note: Diagram and browser checks establish presentation behavior only. No production runtime or measured customer benefit is established here.

slides.title: Put the product inside the delivery plan.
slides.lead: Use the seven-stage journey to govern this proposal. Reuse existing solutions before building another component.

items.title: Intake + requirements
items.text: Name the workflow and owners. Reuse catalog components. Map sources, baseline cost and success criteria.

items.title: Product design
items.text: Approve the context contract, Metric Passport, review duties, success gates and pilot budget.

items.title: Development
items.text: Build one complete context path. Reuse LookML and verify one consumer adapter.

items.title: Testing
items.text: Check owner-approved gold truth, standing QA, permissions and cost. Require security and leadership go/no-go.

items.title: Launch
items.text: Publish only the accepted release. Confirm operating owners, support and rollback.

items.title: Maintenance
items.text: Review corrections and drift. Requalify source or model changes before expanding.

slides.note: Seven stages: intake/vetting, product requirements, product design, development, testing, launch and maintenance. Proposed mapping to the supplied plan. ERP or warehouse replacement is outside scope.

slides.eyebrow: Build path · one complete vertical slice
slides.title: Build the smallest complete proof of the product.
slides.lead: Begin with one real context record and one consuming application. Complete the whole path before widening coverage.

items.title: Agree the contract
items.text: Reuse existing solutions. Set source bindings, reviewer authority, output schema and success gates.

items.title: Implement admission
items.text: Use one custom-app workflow to submit, review, version and persist an approved record.

items.title: Link and publish
items.text: Build its layer references and publish an atomic approved release.

items.title: Consume securely
items.text: Verify one consumer adapter. Check identity, permissions and bounded context delivery.

items.title: Test failure paths
items.text: Exercise rejection, conflict, withdrawal, expiry and failed publication.

items.title: Measure and decide
items.text: Compare accepted-task cost, quality and latency. Expand only after owner acceptance.

slides.note: This is a proposed development sequence. Scope, schedule, hosting, pricing and commitments require an agreed pilot contract.

slides.title: Approve a bounded proof of value.
slides.lead: Approve the pilot scope before development. Start with one governed metric, one reviewer and one existing consuming application.

items.title: Pilot deliverable
items.text: A reusable context release linked to LookML, plus replayable acceptance evidence.

items.title: Buyer contribution
items.text: One workflow, source owner, baseline, reviewer time and permitted test access.

items.title: Investment decision
items.text: Approve a setup ceiling, recurring budget and named delivery responsibilities.

items.title: Expansion decision
items.text: Accept the result only when economics, quality and control meet the agreed gates.

slides.note: Approval funds a scoped pilot. Expansion requires a separate evidence-based decision. Price, dates and thresholds remain to agree.

slides.title: A failure must not silently become approved context.
slides.lead: Implement explicit holds and traceable decisions at each boundary.

items.title: Invalid or missing evidence
items.text: Reject malformed data. Hold unsupported claims for revision.

items.title: Uncertain or conflicting meaning
items.text: Record the conflict. Ask the responsible reviewer.

items.title: Changed approved record
items.text: Require a new version and review. Keep the prior audit history.

items.title: Expired or withdrawn input
items.text: Invalidate dependent output and cached views.

items.title: Denied consumer access
items.text: Return a controlled denial. Do not leak restricted record content.

items.title: Publication failure
items.text: Keep the prior release available. Do not expose a partial update.

slides.note: Proposed acceptance behaviors. The implementation must prove them with durable readback and failure tests.

slides.title: Inspect the foundations behind the proposal.
slides.lead: Standards and platform documentation support the proposal. They do not establish runtime acceptance or business return.
slides.note: The supplied v6 planning reference informs stack and journey alignment. It is not a measured product result or an approved optimization policy.

pitch.audience: Enterprise AI leaders, operations owners and pilot sponsors

lenses.name: Cost
lenses.mechanism: Bound context size. Reuse valid views. Choose a capable route.
lenses.measure: All-in recurring cost per accepted task, plus one-time setup cost.
lenses.guardrail: Include review, rework, retrieval and operations. Token savings alone do not establish value.

lenses.name: Performance
lenses.mechanism: Use bounded decisions and fast paths. Escalate when the task needs more work.
lenses.measure: End-to-end median and p95 latency, throughput and retries at agreed load.
lenses.guardrail: p95 is the time within which 95% of measured tasks finish. Compare the same workload and quality gates.

lenses.name: Accuracy
lenses.goal: Preserve the meaning behind the answer
lenses.mechanism: Carry source links, dates, conditions and conflicts. Check derived statements.
lenses.measure: Domain-reviewed task acceptance, supported claims and appropriate abstention.
lenses.guardrail: Abstention means withholding a conclusion when evidence is insufficient. A correct format does not prove a correct answer.

lenses.name: Trust
lenses.mechanism: Enforce scope and permission. Show the evidence, owner and review decision.
lenses.measure: Boundary-test results, audit coverage, owner approval and user confidence.
lenses.guardrail: Measure user confidence separately from correctness. Model confidence cannot create authority.

scorecard.name: Cost
scorecard.metric: Recurring cost per accepted task; one-time setup; maintenance effort.
scorecard.trial: Compare the same accepted-task target. Record token and query charges, allocated and incremental licenses, adapters, operations and human handling without double counting.
scorecard.decision: Expand only when the agreed economic case holds after full cost readback.

scorecard.name: Performance
scorecard.metric: Median and p95 completion time; throughput; retries; recovery time.
scorecard.trial: Measure submit-to-approved-delivery latency and consuming-task completion separately. Include review queues and p95 at agreed load.
scorecard.decision: Meet the owner’s service target without hiding failed, queued or held tasks.

scorecard.name: Accuracy
scorecard.metric: Task acceptance; source correctness; stale/conflict detection; abstention.
scorecard.trial: Test held-out questions against approved LookML definitions and owner-reviewed gold truth. Check grain, unit, time window and exceptions.
scorecard.decision: Meet agreed quality gates. Investigate failures before expanding scope.

scorecard.name: Trust
scorecard.metric: Scope isolation; permission enforcement; evidence coverage; reviewer decisions.
scorecard.trial: Test source and consumer access, revoked permissions, hostile instructions, cross-vault retrieval and exact-version audit readback.
scorecard.decision: Hold release for a material access failure. Assess user confidence separately.

businessCase.definition: Compare the same monthly target of accepted tasks. Acceptance means the owner confirms the task and quality criteria.
businessCase.formula: Attempts = accepted target / acceptance rate. Recurring cost = attempts × (digital cost + handling minutes × hourly rate / 60) + fixed cost. Year-one net = 12 × monthly difference − setup.
businessCase.limitation: Invented example assumptions, not a quote or measured savings. The neutral starting case assumes no improvement. Rates and workload stay constant for the annual estimate. Validate the inputs and all quality gates.
businessCase.costScope: Digital cost includes model tokens, retrieval, warehouse queries, tools and variable infrastructure per attempt. Handling includes review, rework and escalation. Fixed cost includes seats, licenses, adapters and operations. Compare existing and incremental costs consistently; count each once. Setup stays separate.

architecture.review: Human approval binds to exact versions. New meaning and feedback return through preparation and review.
architecture.legend: Solid arrows: approved processing and delivery. Dashed arrows: revision or new submission. IDs connect layers; IDs grant no permission.

stages.title: Submit, prepare and review
stages.detail: Preserve the original. Check schema, evidence and STE-inspired meaning. Human reviewers approve, reject or request changes to the exact version.

stages.title: Register and organize approved context
stages.detail: Resolve canonical identities and versions. The harness asks the chosen model for typed decisions. It places approved records; new meaning returns through preparation and review.

stages.title: Link the semantic layers
stages.detail: Organize Data, Metric, Ontology and Interpretation records in a controlled workspace. Derived objects retain their own IDs and references to approved input versions.

stages.title: Publish and deliver permitted context
stages.detail: Publish a complete validated release. The MCP server checks caller and record access. Consumers receive IDs, evidence and current versions, and control their own actions.

stages.title: Review feedback and corrections
stages.detail: Consumer feedback and new agent interpretations start submissions. Human approval never happens automatically. Expiry, withdrawal or access changes invalidate dependent outputs.

submission.check: Review new IDs and derived meaning.
